A hieroglyph is a single picture-symbol used as a unit of writing — where a drawn image of something (a bird, an eye, a hand, a wavy line) stands for a word, a sound, or an idea, instead of a letter of an alphabet.

Think of it this way: in English, you write the word "sun" using three letters — s, u, n. In a hieroglyphic writing system, you might instead draw a circle with rays coming out of it, and that picture itself becomes the written word. That single picture-symbol is one hieroglyph.

The plural form is hieroglyphs. When you refer to the entire system of writing made up of these symbols, you can call it hieroglyphics (though that's more of a collective or adjective use — more on that below).

When people say "hieroglyphs," they almost always mean the ones used by the ancient Egyptians — those beautiful, intricate symbols carved into the walls of temples and pyramids, painted inside tombs, and written on rolls of papyrus (a kind of paper made from a reed plant). Ancient Egyptian hieroglyphs are the most famous example in the world.

But strictly speaking, the word isn't limited to Egypt. Any system of writing that uses pictures or pictorial symbols as its characters can be called hieroglyphic, and each symbol in it is a hieroglyph. Similar picture-writing systems existed in other ancient civilizations too — the Hittites, the Mayans, and others — and their symbols can also technically be called hieroglyphs.
How a Single Hieroglyph Actually Works

This is where it gets interesting. A hieroglyph doesn't work in just one fixed way — a single symbol could be doing one of three different jobs depending on context:

1. It can represent a thing directly (a "word-sign").
A picture of a mouth could simply mean "mouth." The image = the object. This is the most intuitive use.

2. It can represent a sound (a "sound-sign").
Here's where it gets clever. Ancient Egyptians often used a picture not for what it showed, but for the sound of what it showed. For example, if the Egyptian word for "mouth" started with the sound r, then the picture of a mouth could be used to write the r sound in an entirely different word — one that has nothing to do with mouths. This is similar to a rebus puzzle, where you might draw a picture of a "bee" + a picture of a "leaf" to write the word "belief."

3. It can serve as a silent classifier (a "determinative").
Some hieroglyphs were placed at the end of a word not to be read aloud, but purely to tell the reader what category the word belongs to. A small picture of a man might be placed after a word to signal "this word refers to a male person." It adds meaning without adding sound.

A complete piece of Egyptian writing would mix all three types together fluidly, and a skilled reader had to know which role each symbol was playing in any given instance.

Egyptian hieroglyphs are remarkably detailed and artistic. There are hundreds of distinct symbols. Some common categories include:

  • People and body parts — a seated man, a walking figure, an eye, a hand, a foot, a mouth
  • Animals — an owl, a lion, a snake, a vulture, a scarab beetle, a fish, a swallow
  • Plants — a lotus flower, a papyrus stem, a tree
  • Objects — a bread loaf, a pot, a knife, a sail, a throne, a sun disk
  • Abstract shapes — wavy lines (water), a semicircle, a folded cloth

Each hieroglyph was a small picture, often drawn with great care and artistic detail. They could be written left-to-right, right-to-left, or top-to-bottom. One clever rule for reading direction: the animal and human figures always face toward the beginning of the line, so you read in the direction they're looking.
Hieroglyphs Were Deciphered, Not Always Known

For over a thousand years after ancient Egyptian civilization declined, nobody could read hieroglyphs anymore. The knowledge had been completely lost. They were just mysterious, beautiful pictures on walls that no one understood. It wasn't until 1822 that a French scholar named Jean-François Champollion cracked the code, largely thanks to the Rosetta Stone — a slab of rock discovered in Egypt that had the same text written in three scripts: hieroglyphs, another Egyptian script, and ancient Greek. Since scholars could already read Greek, they used it as a key to decode the hieroglyphs.
The Word in Everyday Modern Use

Over time, the word "hieroglyph" has taken on a looser, informal meaning in everyday language. People sometimes use it to describe any writing or symbols they can't read or understand — especially if it looks complex, foreign, or indecipherable.

For example, someone might say: "I can't read the doctor's handwriting — it looks like hieroglyphs to me." Here, they don't literally mean ancient Egyptian picture-writing. They mean: it's so hard to read that it might as well be a mysterious ancient script. This is a figurative, casual use of the word.

So "hieroglyph" in modern informal use can simply mean: a symbol or piece of writing that is completely unintelligible to the person looking at it.
Hieroglyph vs. Hieroglyphics — A Common Point of Confusion

These two words are closely related but used slightly differently:

  • Hieroglyph (noun) = one single symbol. "The hieroglyph depicting an owl represented the sound 'm'."
  • Hieroglyphics (noun, used as a plural or collective) = the entire writing system, or all the symbols together. "The tomb walls were covered in hieroglyphics."

You might also hear hieroglyphic used as an adjective: "hieroglyphic script," "hieroglyphic inscriptions."

In practice, people often use "hieroglyphics" loosely even when talking about individual symbols, and that's generally accepted in casual speech. But if you want to be precise: one symbol = a hieroglyph; the whole system or a collection of symbols = hieroglyphics.

A hieroglyph is a picture-symbol used as a unit of writing, where the image represents a word, a sound, or a category — rather than being a letter. The term most commonly refers to the ancient Egyptian writing system, one of the oldest and most sophisticated in human history, though it can apply to any similar picture-based script. Each symbol is carefully crafted and can function in multiple ways within a piece of writing. In modern informal use, the word is also borrowed to describe any writing or symbols that look impossibly complex or unreadable.
